---
title: "Week 3 self-check — measurements and variation"
---

Explain the quantities before calculating. Use these checks to identify what to
practise again; they are not an assessment. Keep the
[statistics reference](../reference/statistics.qmd) nearby.

## 1. Mean, variance, and SD

Three growth measurements are 12, 14, and 16 mm. What are the mean, sample
variance, and sample SD? Show the units.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked answer

Mean = **14 mm**. Deviations are −2, 0, and 2 mm; squared deviations sum to 8.
Divide by `n − 1 = 2` to obtain sample variance **4 mm²**. Its square root is
sample SD **2 mm**. SD describes spread among these measurements, not the
uncertainty in their mean.
:::

## 2. A common shift and a unit conversion

If every measurement above gains 10 mm, what happens to mean and SD? If the
original lengths are converted from mm to cm, how do mean, SD, and variance change?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and check

Adding 10 shifts the mean to **24 mm** but leaves SD at **2 mm**, since deviations
from the mean are unchanged. Dividing lengths by ten gives mean **1.4 cm**,
SD **0.2 cm**, and variance **0.04 cm²**. Variance scales by the square of the
conversion factor.
:::

## 3. An unusual number is a question, not proof of an error

The messy table contains final length 4.38 for P21. What permits correcting it
to 43.8 mm? What should happen to the unavailable final measurement for P06?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and check

The supplied source notes confirm a transcription/unit error and give **43.8 mm**.
The unusual value alone would not justify multiplying by ten. P06 remains
missing because there is no supported replacement in this exercise. Preserve
the raw file and record repairs in code; zero would invent a measurement.
:::

## 4. Rows versus available measurements

After the confirmed identical duplicate is removed, the repaired table has
24 plants and one unavailable growth value in the control group. How many
plant records and available growth measurements are there per group?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and check

There are **12 control and 12 treated plant records**, but **11 control and
12 treated available growth measurements**. The complete clean seedling file
used later is a separate teaching dataset with 12 available per group. State
which file the analysis uses, and do not silently mix those counts.
:::

## 5. More readings or more independent units?

One treated plant is measured twelve times. A second study independently
assigns twelve plants to treatment. Are these equivalent sources of information
about differences among plants?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and check

No. Repeated readings of one plant may reveal measurement consistency but do
not create twelve independently treated plants. The design determines the
experimental unit. Likewise, reweighing one synthesis run does not create more
independently prepared runs.
:::

## 6. Spread of observations versus spread of sample means

The supplied simulation draws means from samples of four or sixteen plants
from the same fixed toy population. Why can the means of sixteen spread less
without changing the population's individual SD?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and check

The source measurements stay the same. A mean averages independent sampling
variation, so repeated means based on more observations typically vary less.
The SD among repeated sample means describes sampling variability of an estimate;
it is not SD among individual plants. A precise estimate can still be biased
or based on an inappropriate design.
:::

## 7. A duplicate identifier needs a design check

A file has two rows with the same plant ID. Is deleting one automatically justified? How does the answer differ between one row per plant and one row per time point?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

No. First establish the intended row meaning and compare the complete records. In the supplied messy exercise, an identical duplicate import is confirmed by source notes. In a repeated-time design, the same plant ID can legitimately recur. Different readings attached to one ID require investigation, not arbitrary deletion.
:::

## 8. What did the invented zero do?

P06 initially measured24.7 mm and has no final reading. A student substitutes final length0. What growth does this calculate, and why is it different from retaining NA?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

It invents −24.7 mm growth. NA states that growth cannot be calculated from the available record; zero final length asserts a measured final size. Omitting an explicitly counted missing value in an available-case mean does not authorise making up a zero measurement.
:::

## 9. Same mean, different spread in a new source

The transfer study has a larger treated mean but a smaller treated SD. Is that inconsistent? What should the axis and summary table say?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

It is consistent: centre and individual spread describe different features. Use seven-day growth in mm, available n=9 per group, and the actual group summaries. Do not copy the first study pattern, where the treated SD was larger, into the second study.
:::

## 10. Read the units after a transformation

A vector has SD 2 mm and variance 4mm². What happens to SD and variance if every value is divided by 10 to express cm? What if10 mm is added to every value instead?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

Conversion gives SD 0.2 cm and variance 0.04cm². A common additive shift changes the mean but neither deviations nor SD/variance. The physical spread did not diminish merely because its unit changed.
:::

## 11. Two simulation settings

One run draws 12 values for each mean and repeats that400 times. Another draws 12 values and repeats1000 times. Did the second acquire more independently measured plants or reduce the sample size of each mean?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

Neither. The source observations and 12 draws per sample stay fixed. More repetitions give a more stable picture of the simulated sampling distribution. Increasing the number of independent draws per estimated mean is a different change from collecting more simulation repetitions.
:::

## 12. Repair a descriptive conclusion

A report says: “The higher group mean proves every treated plant improved; the SD is the 95% uncertainty.” Repair the two errors without adding a test.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

A greater observed mean can coexist with overlapping individuals, so describe the group tendency and observations. SD describes individual spread, not a95% confidence interval. A descriptive report should state outcome, units, n, centre, spread and limits rather than inventing inferential or universal claims.
:::
